unit_label: Module A: International Banking - Correspondent Banking and NRI Accounts

facts.statement: RTGS stands for Real Time Gross Settlement: instructions are processed as they are received and each transfer is settled individually, without netting. Settlement takes place in the books of the Reserve Bank of India, so payments are final and irrevocable.

The RTGS system is primarily meant for large value transactions. The minimum amount to be remitted through RTGS is Rs 2,00,000 with no upper or maximum ceiling, and RBI sets no amount cap. RTGS is available on all days on a 24x7x365 basis (since 14 December 2020).
facts.locator: FAQ 6 and the benefits answer; availability date corroborated by S03 printed p. 68

facts.statement: NEFT is a nation-wide centralised payment system owned and operated by the Reserve Bank of India. It operates in batches at half-hourly intervals and is available round the clock on all days of the year (24x7x365).
RBI imposes no limit on the amount that can be transferred through NEFT; a member bank may place amount limits based on its own risk perception with the approval of its Board.

A person without a bank account may remit through NEFT by depositing cash at an NEFT-enabled branch with additional details such as complete address and telephone number; such cash remittances are restricted to a maximum of Rs 50,000 per transaction.
A beneficiary's account should be credited within two hours of the NEFT batch settlement.

CHAPS payments between direct participants are settled individually on a gross basis in the Bank of England's real-time gross settlement system and are irrevocable. The courseware (S03 printed p. 67) says CHAPS works on net settlement principles like CHIPS.
facts.locator: How does CHAPS work; compare S03 printed p. 67, section 3.4.4

payload.title: RTGS: large payments, settled one by one
payload.core_explanation_md:
**RTGS** (Real Time Gross Settlement) is the Reserve Bank's system for large-value rupee transfers between banks.

Read the name word by word:
- **Real time**: an instruction is processed the moment it arrives.
- **Gross**: every payment is settled on its own, never netted against another.
- **Settlement**: it happens in the books of the Reserve Bank, so banks move funds through their accounts with it, and a settled payment is **final and irrevocable**.

Three facts to remember for the exam:
1. **Floor**: ₹2,00,000 is the minimum for a single remittance.
2. **Ceiling**: none set by RBI.
3. **Hours**: every day, around the clock (24x7x365), since 14 December 2020.

payload.title: NEFT: batches every half hour, round the clock
payload.core_explanation_md:
**NEFT** (National Electronic Funds Transfer) is a centralised system owned and run by the Reserve Bank. Unlike RTGS it does not settle each payment on arrival: payments are collected and settled in **batches at half-hourly intervals**, and it works every day of the year, around the clock.

- **Size of payment**: RBI sets no limit. A member bank may set its own limits, based on its risk view and with its Board's approval.
- **Credit to the beneficiary**: expected within two hours of the batch settlement.
- **Without an account**: a person with no bank account can send money by depositing cash at an NEFT-enabled branch, giving address and telephone details, but only up to ₹50,000 per transaction.

Contrast with RTGS: NEFT has no floor at ₹2,00,000 and settles in batches, RTGS settles one by one.

payload.title: Three payments, which rail?
payload.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: a branch has three customer transfers to other banks today: (A) ₹1,50,000; (B) ₹2,00,000; (C) ₹12,40,000. Which can go by RTGS, and which by NEFT?

worked_steps.description: Recall the RTGS floor: a single remittance must be at least this amount.

worked_steps.intermediate_result: A is below the floor: not eligible for RTGS

worked_steps.description: Compare B: equal to the floor is enough.
NEFT has no RBI floor or ceiling, so all three can go by NEFT, subject to the sending bank's own limits.
worked_steps.intermediate_result: A, B and C can all use NEFT

payload.final_answer_with_unit: A: NEFT only. B and C: RTGS or NEFT (RTGS if immediate, individual settlement is wanted, NEFT otherwise)

self_check.expected_takeaway: A member bank may set its own amount limits, based on its risk view and with Board approval.

payload.title: A caution on CHAPS: the textbook and the Bank of England differ
payload.core_explanation_md:
The courseware describes CHAPS, the sterling system in London, as working like CHIPS on a **net** settlement principle.

The Bank of England, which operates CHAPS, describes it differently: payments between direct participants are settled **individually, on a gross basis**, in its real-time gross settlement system, and are irrevocable.

What to do with this:
- Treat CHAPS as the British high-value sterling system, with TARGET2 and Fedwire as the euro and dollar real-time gross systems.
- Do not rely on the net-versus-gross label for CHAPS alone. If an exam statement says CHAPS nets like CHIPS, it follows the courseware wording; the operator's own description is gross.
- CHIPS is the one of the group that nets.

self_check.prompt_text: Which of CHIPS, Fedwire, TARGET2 and CHAPS does the operator itself describe as netting?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Only CHIPS. The others are described by their operators as gross settlement.
